newsitem.title: USA: US administration rejects nuke waste bill changes.
newsitem.headline: US administration rejects nuke waste bill changes.

text.p: Energy Secretary Federico Pena said Thursday that changes made in a Senate bill to build a storage dump in Nevada for nuclear waste from power plants were not good enough to win the White House's support.
"Generally speaking, as far as I have seen the changes, the bill is still not acceptable to the administration," Pena told Reuters on his way out of a House national security subcomittee hearing.

The White House has threatened to veto the bill, which would force the government to build a dump to store spent fuel at the Nevada Test Site, if it decides next year that it could eventually bury the waste safely in the nearby Yucca Mountain.

The Republican sponsors of the bill Wednesday agreed to change the bill to defer the opening of the storage facility to 2003, shrink its proposed size, and let the Environmental Protection Agency set the allowable radiation standard for it.

Nuclear utilities are pressing for a temporary storage site until the government has a permanent dump ready to bury their waste. Under law, the Energy Department is supposed to start taking responsibility for the waste by February 1998.
But the government has nowhere to put it yet and does not expect to have a permanent dump ready until 2010 at the earliest. The only site under investigation as a permanent dump is Yucca Mountain.

Under the bill, if the government decided that Yucca Mountain would not make a safe permanent dump, then the government would have to find another site to park the thousands of tons of waste until it does have a dump ready.

In debate Thursday, the Senate approved two amendments that would bar the government from storing the waste at the Energy Department's Savannah River plant in South Carolina or its Oak Ridge site in Tennessee.
Senators rejected an amendment that would have taken out those exceptions and an exception for the Energy Department's Hanford site in Oregon.

The Senate also rejected an amendment that aimed to free the Energy Department of any blame for failing to fulfill the contract to take utilities' waste in 1998, and shield the government from having to pay damages under a pending lawsuit.
A final vote on the bill has been scheduled for April 15.
An Energy Department official said the administration was reluctant to comment on what changes it might find acceptable because the whole bill was in flux.

Instead, Pena said he was focused on talks with utilities, states and other groups to find a way to resolve the lawsuit filed by utilities and states which have already paid the government more than $10 billion to take away their waste.
"I'm trying to craft some realistic responses to the immediate concern that people have about our inability to comply with our contract in January of 1998," he said.
